primitives.name: Marginal Price Equilibrium
primitives.verbatim_quote: 120 RISK, UNCERTAINTY, AND PROFIT At a moment, the theoretical price of any good is the ("marginal") demand price of the existing supply, the highest uniform price that will take the supply out of the market.
primitives.assumptions: Supply is fixed, demand is a function of price; market clears at P where Q_s = Q_d.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When Q_s > Q_d, excess supply drives P downward; when Q_s < Q_d, excess demand drives P upward.

layer2.mapping: GSI Bayesian inference maps marginal price to posterior belief over supply-demand states; GSE state transition models price drift toward equilibrium.
layer2.telemetry: Observed price convergence to equilibrium point via supply-demand mismatch signals.

primitives.name: Dynamic Supply Adjustment
primitives.verbatim_quote: The supply of any particular good may change freely and will do so as its price varies, other things being equal.
primitives.assumptions: Supply is responsive to price changes; production capacity adjusts with price fluctuations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Supply becomes inelastic or non-responsive at extreme price levels due to resource constraints.

layer2.mapping: GSE models supply elasticity as a feedback kernel in production-consumption dynamics; GSI infers supply sensitivity from observed price-response patterns.
layer2.telemetry: Rate of supply change relative to price variation across time series.

primitives.name: Production-Consumption Balance
primitives.verbatim_quote: The price must be adjusted not to dispose of a fixed supply, but to equate a rate 1 of production with a rate of consumption, both variable with or "functions of" the price.
primitives.assumptions: Production and consumption rates vary with price; equilibrium occurs when R_p = R_c.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Imbalance leads to price drift until R_p = R_c, indicating market disequilibrium.

layer2.mapping: GSI Bayesian model uses production-consumption functions to infer latent price drivers; GSE simulates balance states through iterative feedback loops.
layer2.telemetry: Deviation of R_p from R_c over time as proxy for market disequilibrium.

reasoning_traces.think:
The marginal price equilibrium primitive defines price as the intersection of fixed supply and varying demand, forming a static snapshot of market clearing. Dynamic supply adjustment introduces variability into this framework by allowing supply to respond to price changes, enabling a more realistic model of market evolution. Production-consumption balance extends this further by treating both rates as functions of price, creating a feedback loop where price adjusts to align these flows. These primitives form a hierarchy: static equilibrium provides baseline, dynamic supply adds responsiveness, and production-consumption balance introduces temporal consistency. Failure modes include rigid supply assumptions leading to persistent disequilibrium, or misaligned production-consumption functions causing oscillatory behavior. The interplay of these operators enables modeling of both short-term price movements and long-run adjustments in supply conditions.
